# A mouse in the elevated plus maze {#sec-movement-mouse}

In this case study, we'll use [`movement`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/) to analyse a mouse navigating an [elevated plus maze (EPM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevated_plus_maze)—a widely used behavioural assay for measuring anxiety in rodents.
Our goal is to quantify how much time the mouse spends in each region of the maze.

We assume you are already familiar with the `movement` dataset structure and the `movement` GUI, both introduced in @sec-movement-intro.

::: {.callout-note title="Using the right environment"}

If you are following along this chapter on your own computer,
make sure to run all code snippets with the `animals-in-motion-env` environment activated
(see [prerequisites @sec-install-movement]). This also applies to launching the
`movement` graphical user interface (@sec-movement-gui).

:::

```{python}
#| include: false
import xarray as xr

xr.set_options(
    display_expand_attrs=False,
    display_expand_coords=False,
    keep_attrs=True,
)
```

## The elevated plus maze

The EPM consists of two open arms and two closed arms (enclosed by walls) arranged in a plus shape, elevated above the ground.
Because of the general aversion of mice to open, exposed spaces, mice tend to prefer the closed arms of the maze.
The proportion of time spent in the open arms is therefore commonly used as a measure of anxiety-like behaviour: the more time spent in the open arms, the less anxious the mouse.

::: {.callout-note title="Acknowledgement"}
Thanks to Loukia Katsouri for sharing this dataset with us.
:::

Let's start by importing everything we'll need.
Besides the usual suspects, we will use four parts of the `movement` API:
[`movement.sample_data`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.sample_data.html) to fetch the data,
[`movement.filtering`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.filtering.html) to clean it,
[`movement.plots`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.plots.html) to visualise where the mouse spent its time,
and [`movement.roi`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.html) to define and analyse regions of the maze.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from movement import sample_data
from movement.filtering import filter_by_confidence, rolling_filter
from movement.plots import plot_occupancy
from movement.roi import compute_region_occupancy, load_rois
```

## Load and inspect the data

In @sec-movement-intro we loaded pose tracks from a file on disk.
Here we'll instead use one of `movement`'s [sample datasets](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/user_guide/input_output.html#target-sample-data)—a curated collection of tracking outputs from various species and software, which are downloaded on demand and cached under `~/.movement/data`.

We fetch the EPM dataset with
[`fetch_dataset()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.sample_data.fetch_dataset.html),
passing `with_video=True` so that the associated video is downloaded as well—we'll need it later.

```{python}
ds = sample_data.fetch_dataset(
    "DLC_single-mouse_EPM.predictions.h5", with_video=True
)
ds
```

These are [DeepLabCut](https://www.mackenziemathislab.org/deeplabcut) predictions for a single mouse, with 8 keypoints tracked over roughly 10 minutes at 30 fps.

Along with the pose tracks, this sample dataset comes with a video and a still frame extracted from it.
Their paths are stored as attributes of the dataset:

```{python}
print(ds.frame_path)
print(ds.video_path)
```

Take note of these paths—we'll need them when we draw regions of interest in the GUI.

## Clean the data

Pose estimation output inevitably contains low-confidence or erroneous predictions, especially around occluded body parts.
In this dataset the mouse is often partly hidden by the walls of the closed arms, so some cleaning is in order before we analyse its position.

We covered the tools for this in @sec-movement-intro, so this time you get to apply them yourself.

::: {.exercise-prompt}
Clean the pose tracks:

1. Discard predictions with a confidence score below `0.95`, using
   [`filter_by_confidence()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.filtering.filter_by_confidence.html).
   Which keypoint loses the most data, and does that make sense given the maze?
2. Smooth the result with a rolling median filter, using
   [`rolling_filter()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.filtering.rolling_filter.html).

Call the cleaned position array `position_clean`—we'll use it for the rest of the chapter.
:::

::: {.exercise-solution}
```{python}
position_conf = filter_by_confidence(
    ds.position, ds.confidence, threshold=0.95, print_report=True
)

position_clean = rolling_filter(
    position_conf, window=5, statistic="median", min_periods=2
)
```

The `snout` is the worst affected, followed by `tail_end` and the two lateral keypoints.
These are the keypoints most likely to disappear behind the walls of the closed arms, or to be obscured when the mouse rears or grooms.
:::

## Visualise space occupancy

Before defining any regions, it's worth getting a global impression of where the mouse spent its time.

In @sec-movement-intro we relied on `xarray`'s built-in plotting methods.
The [`movement.plots`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.plots.html) module adds a few plotting functions on top of those, tailored to motion tracking data.
One of them is
[`plot_occupancy()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.plots.plot_occupancy.html),
which draws a 2D histogram of position—by default for the centroid of all keypoints, aggregated over all individuals.

We'll overlay the histogram on the still frame that came with the dataset, so we can see the maze underneath.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-epm-occupancy
#| fig-cap: "Occupancy of the mouse's centroid across the maze, on a logarithmic colour scale."

frame = plt.imread(ds.frame_path)
height, width = frame.shape[:2]

# Bins of 30x30 pixels, covering the whole frame
bin_size = 30
bins = [
    np.arange(0, width + bin_size, bin_size),
    np.arange(0, height + bin_size, bin_size),
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(frame)

plot_occupancy(
    position_clean,
    ax=ax,
    bins=bins,
    alpha=0.8,
    cmin=10,  # hide bins with fewer than 10 frames
    norm="log",
)

# Match the axes to the frame, keeping the image orientation
ax.set_xlim(0, width)
ax.set_ylim(height, 0)
ax.set_title("Occupancy heatmap")
ax.collections[0].colorbar.set_label("# frames")
```

Any keyword arguments beyond the first few are passed straight to
[`matplotlib`'s `hist2d`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.hist2d.html),
which is where `bins`, `cmin` and `norm` come from.
The logarithmic colour scale is worth the extra argument here: without it, the few heavily visited bins would flatten everything else to a single colour.

The plus shape of the maze emerges clearly from the data alone, and the centre of the maze stands out as the most visited area.
To say anything about the arms, though, we need to define them explicitly.

## Define ROIs in napari {#sec-epm-napari}

A region of interest (ROI) is a shape in the same pixel coordinates as the tracking data, which we can then ask questions about—for example, whether the mouse was inside it at a given time.
The easiest way to define one is to draw it on top of the video, in the `movement` GUI we met in @sec-movement-gui.

::: {.callout-note}
The steps below are a condensed version of the [define regions of interest](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/user_guide/gui.html#define-regions-of-interest) section of the `movement` GUI guide, which happens to use this very dataset for its screenshots. Refer to the guide for the full details.
:::

1. Launch the GUI from the command line with `movement launch`.
2. Load a background layer: drag and drop either the video or the still frame onto the viewer, using the paths we printed above.
3. Expand the "Define regions of interest" menu on the right-hand side, and click "Add new layer". This adds a napari [shapes layer](https://napari.org/stable/howtos/layers/shapes.html) named "regions", managed by `movement`.
4. With that layer selected, press <kbd>P</kbd> to activate the polygon tool and draw around one region of the maze, clicking once per vertex. Each shape you draw appears as a row in the regions table.
5. Repeat until you have five regions: the two open arms (left and right), the two closed arms (top and bottom), and the central square.
6. Double-click the name cell of each row to rename it. We'll use `open_arm_left`, `open_arm_right`, `closed_arm_top`, `closed_arm_bottom` and `centre`.
7. Click "Save layer" and save the regions to a `.geojson` file.

::: {.callout-note title="Shapes and regions"}
Any napari shape can become a `movement` region, but the resulting type depends on what you drew:
polygons, rectangles and ellipses become
[`PolygonOfInterest`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.PolygonOfInterest.html) objects,
while lines and paths become
[`LineOfInterest`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.LineOfInterest.html) objects.
The latter are useful for boundaries an animal may cross, rather than areas it may occupy.
:::

Where you place the boundaries between the arms and the centre is a judgement call, and it will affect the numbers we compute below—something to keep in mind when comparing results across studies.

## Load and visualise ROIs

Regions saved from the GUI are read back into Python with
[`load_rois()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.load_rois.html).
So that the rest of this chapter runs regardless of what you drew, we'll use a set of regions we prepared earlier and stored in the book's repository.

```{python}
rois = load_rois("data/EPM_rois.geojson")

[roi.name for roi in rois]
```

We get back a list of region objects, each carrying its name and its vertices:

```{python}
print(rois[0])
```

Every region can draw itself onto a `matplotlib` axes with its
[`plot()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.PolygonOfInterest.html#movement.roi.PolygonOfInterest.plot)
method, so we can check that our regions line up with the maze.

```{python}
#| label: fig-epm-rois
#| fig-cap: "The five regions of interest drawn over the EPM."

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(frame)

for roi, colour in zip(rois, plt.cm.Dark2.colors, strict=False):
    roi.plot(ax, facecolor=colour, alpha=0.5)

ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize="small")
```

Plotting is only the simplest thing regions can do.
A `PolygonOfInterest` also knows how to compute the distance from a point to its boundary, the nearest point on that boundary, and the angle at which an animal approaches it—see the [`movement.roi`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.html) API reference and the [boundary angles example](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/examples/boundary_angles.html) for what's possible.
